lessons.title: Common Advance Tax Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

body.text: Almost every advance tax problem in India comes from one of three beliefs: that TDS has handled it, that the ₹10,000 test is about income rather than tax, or that 31 March is the deadline. None of them is true, and each one has a predictable price measured in months of interest.

children.text: You now know the rules. This lesson is about where people trip over them. Each mistake below is common, each one has a cost you can calculate, and each has a fix that takes minutes. Treat it as a checklist to run against your own year before the next due date.

cells: "My employer deducts TDS, so I am covered"
Employer TDS covers only the salary that employer pays, plus anything you declare to payroll
List every income outside your payslip in June and run the ₹10,000 test
"I earn under ₹12 lakh, so advance tax does not apply"
The ₹10,000 test is on tax after TDS, not on income, and the rebate does not cover capital gains
Compute tax first, then subtract TDS, then compare with ₹10,000
"The bank already deducted TDS on my FD"
TDS is 10% while your slab may be 30%: on ₹1,00,000 of interest that leaves ₹21,200 still to pay
Add interest income at your slab rate and subtract only the TDS actually deducted
"I will deal with my share gains when I file"
Gains carry no TDS, and tax on them is due in the instalment after they arise
Check your broker tax P&L before each due date and pay tax on new gains
"I paid what I estimated, so I am safe"
Instalments are tested against the tax on the income you finally return
Revise the estimate at every due date, not just in June
"31 March is the deadline"
The last instalment is due 15 March; paying on 31 March still attracts one month of interest for that instalment
Treat 15 March as the hard date and pay by the 10th
"I switched jobs, payroll will sort it out"
Each employer taxes only its own salary and may apply the standard deduction and rebate twice
Declare your previous salary and TDS to the new employer as soon as you join
"I am over 60, so I am exempt"
The exemption goes the moment you have any business or professional income, including consulting or F&O
Check the three conditions: resident, 60 or over, and no business or professional income
"I use the presumptive scheme, so advance tax does not apply"
Presumptive taxpayers still pay advance tax; they simply pay all of it by 15 March
Set a firm March reminder and set money aside from every receipt
"I paid, so the record will take care of itself"
A wrong year or wrong type of payment on the challan can leave the credit unmatched
Check the receipt, then confirm the credit in AIS or Form 26AS within a week

body.title: The five AIS entries people most often miss

cells: Savings account interest
Small amounts across several banks, with no TDS and no certificate
FD interest accrued but not yet paid out
Cumulative deposits credit interest yearly, so nothing shows in the account
Dividends
Credited directly to the bank account, often in small amounts across many companies
Mutual fund redemptions
Treated as a withdrawal rather than a taxable gain, especially in debt funds and systematic withdrawal plans
Rent reported by a company tenant
Companies deduct TDS on rent, so it is visible to the department even when the landlord forgets it

children.text: Opening AIS once in June, once in December and once before you file catches nearly all of these.
The Cost of the 31 March Myth

The single most common timing mistake is treating 31 March as the advance tax deadline. Money paid by 31 March is still advance tax, and it does protect you from interest for not paying advance tax. What it does not do is satisfy any of the four instalment dates.

body.label: What paying everything on 31 March costs
body.context: Interest for deferment on all four instalments, even though no interest for not paying advance tax applies, since 100% was paid within the tax year.

body.title: Try It: All of It on 31 March
body.prompt: Meera, a Kanpur-based consultant with regular books, owes ₹1,50,000 of tax after TDS for tax year 2026-27. She pays the entire amount on 31 March 2027. What is her total interest under section 425 for the four instalments? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: June: 15% of ₹1,50,000 is ₹22,500, unpaid, for 3 months: ₹675. September: 45% is ₹67,500, for 3 months: ₹2,025. December: 75% is ₹1,12,500, for 3 months: ₹3,375. March: the full ₹1,50,000 was unpaid on 15 March, charged for 1 month: ₹1,500. Total ₹7,575. Because she did pay everything by 31 March, section 424 does not apply.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: What 31 March Saves
body.textWithBlank: Paying the full amount by 31 March protects you from interest under section ___, but not from interest under section 425.
body.explanation: Section 424 asks whether you paid at least 90% of your tax within the tax year, so paying by 31 March satisfies it. Section 425 tests each of the four due dates separately, and 31 March is not one of them.

children.text: One Freelancer, Three Versions of the Same Year
Ravi is a web developer in Coimbatore who keeps regular books. His tax after TDS for tax year 2026-27 is ₹1,20,000 in all three versions below. Only his behaviour changes.

body.title: Interest on the same ₹1,20,000 tax bill

children.text: Paying on schedule costs nothing. Paying the same amount two weeks late, on 31 March, costs ₹6,060, about 5.1% of his tax. Waiting until he files in July costs ₹10,860, or about 9.0%, because interest for not paying advance tax is added on top. The tax itself never changed.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Mistake Costs More?
body.question: Two freelancers each owe ₹2,00,000 of tax after TDS. Anil pays nothing until 15 March, then pays the full amount. Bhavna pays 15%, 45% and 75% on time, then pays the rest on 30 June. Who pays more interest?
options: Anil, because he missed three instalments
Bhavna, because her payment crossed into the next year
Neither, because both paid in full
body.explanation: Anil misses June, September and December, costing 3 months each on 15%, 45% and 75% of ₹2,00,000: ₹900 plus ₹2,700 plus ₹4,500, which is ₹8,100. Bhavna misses only the March instalment: ₹500 on the ₹50,000 balance for 1 month, plus interest for not paying advance tax on that shortfall for 3 months to June, ₹1,500. Her total is ₹2,000. Missing early instalments is usually more expensive than finishing slightly late.

body.title: What people believe, and what the law says

columns.label: The belief
points: Advance tax is only for businesses
If TDS was deducted, nothing more is due
Interest applies only if you file late
Nobody checks small amounts of interest or dividend income

columns.label: The reality
points: It applies to anyone whose tax after TDS reaches ₹10,000, including salaried investors
TDS is a flat-rate deposit, usually below the tax due for higher slabs
Interest applies even when the return is filed on time, if instalments were short
Refund interest is only 0.5% a month, starts on 1 April, and is itself taxable
AIS already carries interest, dividends, securities sales and rent reported by others

body.text: Do not deliberately underpay on the assumption that interest is cheaper than a loan. At 1% a month, interest for not paying advance tax runs at 12% a year on the whole shortfall, interest for deferment adds up to 3 percentage points more per instalment, and none of it is deductible. It is one of the more expensive ways to borrow money in India.

The cheapest advance tax habit is the AIS habit. Most mistakes on this list are failures of information, not arithmetic. Everything the department knows about your interest, dividends, securities sales and TDS is already sitting in AIS. Read it three times a year and most of these mistakes cannot happen to you.

body.title: Scenario: Diagnose Three Taxpayers
body.scenario: Three people describe their year. Sunita, 45, salaried in Delhi: "I sold mutual fund units in July for a ₹4 lakh long-term gain. I will pay the tax when I file next year." Prakash, 62, retired in Mangaluru: "I am a senior citizen, so I am exempt. I do consult for my old company for about ₹6 lakh a year." Ismail, 34, a Hyderabad trader: "My F&O profit is ₹14 lakh, but I paid nothing in June because I had no idea how the year would go."
body.prompt: For each person, name the mistake, say whether interest applies, and give the fix.
body.modelAnswer: Sunita: the mistake is treating capital gains as a filing-season problem. Her gain of ₹4,00,000 is taxed at 12.5% above the ₹1,25,000 exemption, about ₹35,750 with cess, with no TDS. Because it arose in July, the timing relief protects her June instalment only if she pays that tax by 15 September. Waiting until filing costs interest under both section 425 and section 424. Fix: pay by the next due date after any sale. Prakash: the mistake is assuming age alone exempts him. Consulting is professional income, so he loses the senior citizen exemption for the whole year and must pay advance tax on his total tax after TDS, in instalments. Fix: check whether TDS deducted by the company covers his tax, and if not, follow the normal schedule, or use the presumptive scheme if his profession qualifies. Ismail: the mistake is confusing an uncertain estimate with no estimate. F&O profit is business income and gets no timing relief, so his June instalment is tested against his final tax. He should have paid 15% of a reasonable estimate. Fix: revise upwards in September and pay the cumulative 45%, which limits interest to the June shortfall for three months rather than letting it repeat at every date.

body.title: Six Habits That Prevent Nearly All of This
steps: Every June, list all income outside your main payslip and run the ₹10,000 test on tax after TDS
Open AIS in June, in December and again before filing, and reconcile it against your own records
Revise your estimate before each due date rather than reusing the June figure
Pay tax on any capital gain, dividend or windfall by the next due date after it arises
Treat 15 March as the final date, not 31 March, and pay a few days early
After each payment, verify the challan shows the right year and Advance Tax (100), and check the credit in AIS or Form 26AS

body.label: Annual Information Statement: Income Tax Department
body.description: Official guidance on viewing your AIS, which lists interest, dividends, securities transactions, TDS and taxes paid. The single best defence against advance tax mistakes.

10% on FD interest and dividends leaves a gap for anyone in the 20% or 30% slab.
Instalments are tested against the tax on the income you finally return, not your June guess.
Lost entirely if there is any business or professional income, however small.
Reading AIS in June, December and before filing prevents most advance tax errors.

points: Most advance tax errors come from assuming TDS covers everything or that the ₹10,000 test is about income
Paying the full amount on 31 March still costs interest for all four instalments: ₹7,575 on a ₹1,50,000 bill
Missing early instalments usually costs more than finishing slightly late, because interest repeats at each date
Capital gains, dividends and windfalls must be paid by the next due date after they arise to keep the timing relief
Interest for advance tax defaults runs at 12% a year and is not deductible, so it is expensive borrowing
Reading AIS three times a year prevents nearly every mistake on this list
